title: Pentecost and ordinary time
hookLine: after Pentecost comes the long green season, when faith gets lived in the ordinary

cards: Jerusalem again, seven weeks after Easter. The city is full of pilgrims for a Jewish harvest feast, visitors from all over the known world.
Acts says: "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place." Jesus's followers, together in a house.
Then a sound like a rushing wind fills the place, and something like flames rests on each of them.

They pour into the street talking, and the crowd, people from Egypt, Rome, Arabia, Asia, each hears them in their own language. Some are amazed. Others laugh and say they're drunk, at nine in the morning.

teach.b: Start with Pentecost, Greek for fiftieth. It was a Jewish feast first, Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, and Jews still keep it.
Christians remember it as the day the Holy Spirit came, and many call it the birthday of the church. Churches wear red for the fire.
Then comes ordinary time. Ordinary doesn't mean boring. It comes from the Latin for numbered, like ordinal numbers: the Sundays are simply counted, the tenth, the eleventh, the twelfth.
Some churches call them the Sundays after Pentecost, or after Trinity. The color is green, the color of things growing.
It's the longest season of the year, from late spring through summer and fall, about half the calendar. No big feasts, no fasting. Just the Gospels read in order, week after week, and life lived.
That's the point. After the waiting and the birth, the desert, the cross, the empty tomb and the fire, the church year says: now go and live it on a Tuesday.
Paul wrote: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord."

teach.h: GOD AMONG THE POTS AND PANS.
teach.b: In the 1600s, a Carmelite brother named Lawrence worked in his monastery's kitchen, and said he felt as near to God among the pots and pans as at the altar.
So end twelve days on the circle of the year, from Advent's candles to the long green season. The holy days point back to the ordinary ones.

how: Many churches celebrate Pentecost in red, fifty days after Easter, remembering the gift of the Spirit; then comes ordinary time, the long green season of numbered Sundays when the Gospels are read week by week.

o: the weeks of fasting between Easter and Pentecost
the counted Sundays of the church's long green season
the plain weeks when nothing in church is holy

s: ordinary time means the boring part of the year
ordinary means numbered: the Sundays are counted one after another.
Pentecost was a Jewish feast before it was a Christian one
Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover. Jews still keep it.
ordinary time is the shortest season
it's the longest, about half the year, in green.

games.q: you're a pilgrim in Jerusalem. a group of Galileans pours into the street, and you hear them speaking your own language. what does the crowd do?
o: some are amazed, and some mock them as drunk.
games.why: Acts says some were amazed and asked what it meant, while "Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine."

practice: Choose one ordinary task you'll do today anyway, washing dishes, folding laundry, answering email, and picture yourself doing it slowly, with full attention, as if it mattered.
If you pray, offer it to God before you start, as prayer; if you don't, as an act of care for the people it serves.

wordCard.voice: Ordinary time. The long green season of the church year. Ordinary meaning numbered, not boring: faith lived week by week. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the fiftieth day. the feast fifty days after Passover, and after Easter.

carryVoice: Your line: the ordinary is holy. Tomorrow, a new stretch: sabbath and scripture. One hundred twenty days in.
